what_its_for: Imipramine is used to treat depression. It may also be used to help children (age 6 and older) who wet the bed at night. Sometimes doctors prescribe it for other conditions like panic disorder or chronic pain. It belongs to a group of medicines called tricyclic antidepressants, which work by balancing certain natural chemicals in your brain.
how_to_take: Take imipramine exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with a small meal or snack. Swallow the capsule or tablet whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause unpleasant side effects like nausea, headache, or feeling unwell. Your doctor will slowly lower your dose before you stop.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it over time to find the right amount for you. For adults treating depression, doses typically range from 75 mg to 200 mg per day, and in some cases up to 300 mg per day. For children using it for bedwetting, doses are much lower and based on body weight. You may take your total daily dose once at bedtime or split it into smaller doses throughout the day, depending on what your doctor recommends. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are not sure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for advice.
storage: Store imipramine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the label. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking imipramine, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness and raise the risk of serious side effects. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires you to be fully alert until you know how this medicine affects you, because it can cause drowsiness. Avoid standing up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as imipramine can cause a sudden drop in blood pressure, making you feel dizzy or faint. Avoid prolonged exposure to sunlight or tanning beds, as imipramine can make your skin more sensitive to the sun. Use sunscreen and protective clothing when going outside. Avoid taking other medicines that cause drowsiness without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first. Tell all of your doctors and your dentist that you take imipramine before having any surgery or procedures.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the nearest emergency room if you experience: thoughts of suicide or harming yourself, new or worsening depression or anxiety, unusual changes in mood or behavior, fast or irregular heartbeat, chest pain, difficulty breathing, severe dizziness or fainting, seizures, high fever with stiff muscles or confusion (possible signs of a rare but serious condition called serotonin syndrome or neuroleptic malignant syndrome), difficulty urinating, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or any severe allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. Children, teens, and young adults taking antidepressants should be watched closely for any unusual changes in behavior, especially in the first few weeks of treatment or after a dose change.
when_it_works: Imipramine does not work right away. For depression, it may take 2 to 4 weeks before you start to notice some improvement, and it may take up to 6 to 8 weeks to feel the full benefit. For bedwetting in children, results may be seen sooner, sometimes within the first week. It is very important to keep taking the medicine even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults: Imipramine should be used with extra caution in older adults because they are more sensitive to side effects like dizziness, confusion, falls, and heart rhythm changes. Older adults may need a lower dose. Children: This medicine is approved for children age 6 and older only for bedwetting. It is not approved for treating depression in children. Children taking this medicine need close monitoring. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Imipramine may harm an unborn baby and can pass into breast milk. Your doctor will help you weigh the risks and benefits. Heart conditions: Let your doctor know if you have any heart problems, as imipramine can affect heart rhythm. You may need an electrocardiogram (ECG/EKG) before starting treatment.
